entities.name: World Medical Association
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The World Medical Association (WMA) is a pivotal international organization, founded in 1947 in response to the ethical challenges faced by medical professionals in the aftermath of World War II. Headquartered in Ferney-Voltaire, France, the WMA has grown to encompass 115 national medical associations, representing millions of physicians worldwide. Its establishment marked a critical juncture in the global medical community, as it aimed to unite physicians to promote the highest standards in medical ethics and practice, particularly in light of the atrocities witnessed during the war.

Key milestones in the WMA's history include the adoption of the Declaration of Geneva in 1948, a modern take on the Hippocratic Oath, which emphasizes the ethical duties of physicians. The Declaration has been revised multiple times, reflecting the evolving challenges in medical ethics, including issues related to human rights and the rights of patients. Through its advocacy and policy frameworks, the WMA has significantly influenced global health policies and the ethical standards by which medical professionals operate, ensuring that patient welfare remains a priority in medical practice.

The legacy of the World Medical Association extends far beyond its founding. It has fostered a culture of ethical accountability among medical professionals, inspiring subsequent global health initiatives and organizations, such as the World Health Organization (WHO). The WMA's commitment to medical ethics has created a ripple effect, encouraging national associations to adopt similar ethical standards and guidelines, thus shaping the future of medical practice across continents. As one physician remarked, 'The WMA is the conscience of medicine, ensuring that we never forget the lessons of the past.'
